A model change is a much broader intervention than editing one rule in

It can even change latency and cost.

So treat a model swap like any other candidate change:

look at the failures you wanted to improve and the cases

At the top of the hierarchy are settings like temperature
and other sampling parameters.

Modern models sometimes omit the ability to change
these parameters at all.
If present, they can affect how variable the model's outputs are,

but they're usually a poor place to start if your actual problem is
that the agent is missing required information, ignoring a rule,
or calling the wrong tool.

Changing temperature doesn't give the agent a field that isn't there,
it doesn't define what no match means,
and it doesn't add a missing eligibility requirement to the prompt.

Those settings are more useful when the variability itself is part of
what you're trying to improve.

So when you find a failure, try to match the change to the evidence.
If the information is missing or inconsistent, look at the data.

If the agent has information, but the requirement is
unclear, look at the prompt.

If the agent knows what to do, but struggles to carry it out reliably,
check the tools and workflow.

If those layers are working and the task is still too hard,
then consider the model.

And if you find that the problem really is about sampling behavior,
then look at your agent's parameters.

The point is to avoid making a broad change when a smaller one may
